item.title: I stopped manually organizing my ROM files, and my retro gaming setup finally feels frictionless
item.itunes:title: I stopped manually organizing my ROM files, and my retro gaming setup finally feels frictionless
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Emulation is hands-down the best way to experience the seemingly endless library of games on older consoles, but making that happen can feel like a chore at times. You have to set up emulators and organize your games properly, even when you try to simplify it with a solution like EmuDeck.

But I wanted my retro gaming setup to be as frictionless as possible, so I built a system that makes things work for me. Now, whenever I get a new game, it goes into my library automatically with no problems, and it's ready to play.

EmuDeck is still a great starting point

Take most of the work out of it

While you can definitely build and organize your library yourself, EmuDeck is a great solution that makes a big chunk of this project much easier. It was originally made for the Steam Deck, but it works just as well on Windows, and all you need to do is run the installer and wait for it to do its thing.

EmuDeck installs the basic emulators you need, along with Emulation Station (ES-DE), a frontend that makes browsing your games much more pleasant. Emulation Station organizes your games by console, and it offers quick jump and filtering options so you can find games more quickly.

Another thing this does is create the folder structure Emulation Station depends on to categorize all your games. When you set up EmuDeck with the default settings, your C: drive will have an Emulation folder, which then has a roms folder, and then all the folders for each platform you could possibly emulate. You need to place ROMs for each platform in the respective folder, which then lets ES-DE present them to you in a beautiful format.

I emulate every console I wanted as a kid on a single mini PC, and I never have to deal with Windows

Reliving the classics is so easy now

16
By  João Carrasqueira

The problem is that you have to drag your ROMs to the correct folder every time, and it's a pretty large pool of folders, so it can take a while. So then I had to automate the organization part.

Organizing my games became easy

I just let my computer do it for me

This part is where things get really interesting thanks to a program called File Juggler. This is technically a paid application, but you can use the free trial indefinitely, and it's perfect for this situation.

File Juggler automatically moves and organizes your files based on criteria you set, so for this experiment, I just created rules for the platforms I cared about most. Basically, File Juggler scans my Downloads folder, and whenever it finds a file with an extension that matches a known ROM format, it moves it to the appropriate folder.

For example, for NES games, I set it to move any file ending in .nes from the Downloads folder to the C:\Emulation\roms es folder; of course, you'll have to adjust if you changed your ROM directory when setting up EmuDeck. Then just repeat that for the other platforms I play, such as SNES, Nintendo 64, and Game Boy. File Juggler can also scan subdirectories, so if you accidentally extract files into a subfolder, you're still covered.

If you download ROMs from the internet, they often come in ZIP files, so for this to work, I usually have to extract the ROM file first. But this doesn't take much thought. If you use an archive manager like WinRAR or 7-Zip, you can simply right-click a file and choose Extract here to get the raw file directly in the Downloads folder, where File Juggler can take it and move it to the appropriate place. This also works with multiple files, so if you download ROMs in bulk, it makes things even easier.

Admittedly, setting up all these rules can still take a good bit of time, but you only have to do it once, so you get that time back fairly quickly as you download more and more ROMs in the future.

My library is stunning now

All organized and easy to find

With this combination fully set up, it's now easier than ever to enjoy the retro games I want to play. I've always loved how Emulation Station can present these old titles in such a beautiful way. There are tons of themes for ES-DE to let you choose how games are presented, but all of them categorize your games by console, let you create a collection of favorites, or simply show your recently played games so you can quickly get back to where you were.

Once you scrape the metadata for the games in your library, you can add box art, screenshots, and trailers to the UI, making the whole experience feel like a museum honoring these retro titles. It's amazing to experience these games this way in the modern era.

I finally organized my emulator collection, and this free frontend made it feel better than a real console

It makes everything feel natural

2
By  João Carrasqueira

The most annoying part of the process was always moving my ROM files into the correct folder, since I usually ended up juggling two windows to drag and drop, and jumping into the right folder every time was a pain. File Juggler fixes that and lets me stop thinking about where my files are going.

The retro gaming setup of my dreams

If you've been wanting a retro gaming setup that's as frictionless as possible, I'd say this is it. It's perfect for a living room setup, and all you need to do is set ES-DE to launch at boot so you can have a console experience without even touching Windows. You'd only need to use Windows to download new games, and even that's easier with File Juggler.

item.title: Your old router is being rented to cybercriminals, and the FBI knows it
item.itunes:title: Your old router is being rented to cybercriminals, and the FBI knows it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Many tech enthusiasts have a standard drawer of shame or garage shelf full of old tech, including a router that probably hasn't seen a firmware patch in five years but still works fine when plugged in. You might decide to put it to good use by adding it as an extra access point in your home, but according to federal cybersecurity alerts, including explicit warnings from the FBI, abandoned hardware can actually be actively hunted out by threat actors.

Your neglected router isn't just sitting idle. It has likely been quietly compromised, turned into a silent residential proxy node, and rented out to cybercriminals looking to mask their malicious traffic behind your home IP address. Leaving unsupported end-of-life routers plugged into your network is a ticking time bomb. Cybercriminal proxy rings are weaponizing outdated hardware to cloak attacks, turning innocent home networks into proxies for crime.

8 signs it's time to replace your aging networking hardware

You wouldn't expect your PC to work forever, so why are you letting your network hardware run into the ground?

By  Joe Rice-Jones

EOL routers are the prime target

They're easy to attack

Why are end-of-life routers prime targets for this type of cybercrime? Legacy networking gear is so heavily exploited due to the security patch vacuum. When a manufacturer designates a router model as end-of-life (EOL), support essentially stops. This means any critical zero-day vulnerabilities discovered months or years after are essentially left permanently unpatched. This can give hackers a wide-open door and the assurance that nothing will happen in the future to fix it.

There's also the danger of preinstalled remote management. Many legacy routers shipped with remote administration features enabled or vulnerable management daemons that threat actors scan for, exploit, and use to establish persistent root access. Essentially, your ISP wanted to make sure that they were able to control your router from an external point if needed, and now this is a feature that is being completely taken advantage of by hackers and criminals.

There are so many risks to your home

Don't let cybercriminals in

Cybercriminal proxy services can actually monetize your old network bandwidth. They can do this through residential IP masking. Cybercriminals prefer residential IP addresses over commercial data center IPs because traffic originating from a residential home can look a lot more legitimate to security filters. This lets them bypass bot detection systems and rate limits while keeping their IP address private and using yours instead.

They also offer proxy-as-a-service, where they use botnets built from infected end-of-life hardware such as legacy Linksys E-series models like the E1200, E2500, or E1000. Criminals can then run proxy networks where bad actors can rent your home IP addresses by the hour to launch credential stuffing, phishing, and DDoS attacks. Again, they use your IP address as a layer of protection.

This can significantly impact home users, and it's not just an abstract enterprise threat but a direct risk to many households. You might end up with a law enforcement backlash when illegal cyberattacks, threat reconnaissance, or illicit purchases are routed through your compromised residential IP address. Federal investigators or corporate security teams can trace the abuse log straight back to your home connection, and suddenly you'll have the police knocking on your door.

There's also the risk of bandwidth theft and network degradation. While this won't get you in trouble with the law, it can be extremely frustrating as these criminals are quietly siphoning your internet bandwidth in the background in order to tunnel malicious traffic. This can impact your latency and data caps without your knowledge.

Protect your home

Replace your old hardware immediately

Luckily, there are things you can do to protect your perimeter. Obviously, start by auditing your network hardware immediately. Check the lifecycle status of every router, access point, and gateway on your network, and make sure they're still under the manufacturer's support. If the manufacturer no longer pushes security updates, it's probably time to decommission the hardware and replace it with something that's a little bit more protected.

If you can't replace the hardware immediately, disable remote administration on your end-of-life router to block external management access, and reboot the device regularly to disrupt basic in-memory malware persistence scripts.

You can also upgrade to open-source or modern supported stacks by transitioning to modern commercial routers with automatic updates or by flashing old hardware-supported open-source firmware if it's applicable and your hardware permits.

Old routers can be great

Just make sure they are secure

Don't let your garbage be someone else's weapon. In cybersecurity, hardware decay doesn't just mean a device stops working; it can actually become a liability. Keeping an unpatched router plugged into the edge of your network is like leaving your car door wide open with the keys in the ignition. Check your network closet today and pull out any legacy, unsupported routers, wipe them, recycle them properly, and ensure your home perimeter is defended by hardware that still knows how to receive a security patch.

item.title: WizTree scans my entire 1TB drive in less than a second, because it skips the way Windows normally reads files
item.itunes:title: WizTree scans my entire 1TB drive in less than a second, because it skips the way Windows normally reads files
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you've ever tried to figure out what's hogging storage space on your drive, you know it's not exactly a quick process. Windows' default method of scanning your drive is painstakingly slow, often taking a few minutes to map a drive with hundreds of thousands of individual files. Tools like WinDirStat employ this slow method of scanning your storage drives.

In contrast, utilities like WizTree can finish the same job in a matter of 1–3 seconds, thanks to an alternative method of scanning your drive. Even fully-filled 2TB SSDs with millions of files can usually be mapped in under 10 seconds. If you have a relatively empty 1TB SSD like mine, the process finishes almost instantaneously. Once you use WizTree or comparable tools, you'll never go back to the way Windows does it.

I stopped letting Windows Update hoard 20% of my SSD, and gained back real performance

But only because I was already low on space.

By  Hamlin Rozario

Windows takes too long to scan your drive

It reads one file at a time

The reason behind Windows' slow drive scanning is the method it employs. When you use a tool like WinDirStat, it uses the Windows file system API, which means asking the OS to scan one directory at a time. Now, this isn't a big deal when you're casually browsing a single folder, but it becomes a massive operation when you need to map an entire drive.

Even if you have a fast SSD, the read speed won't make a difference, since the bottleneck is the sheer number of individual files. The time to scan a drive scales directly with the number of files and folders on it, and the default API method can take several minutes. Waiting this long just to see what's occupying the most space on your SSD can be frustrating.

I stopped clearing Windows caches after discovering it was silently costing me performance

A few megabytes of storage you'll never notice, or long loading times that you will?

By  Abhinav Raj

WizTree uses a specific trick that bypasses the regular method

The number of files stops being the bottleneck

WizTree completely bypasses slow drive scans by using a database that every NTFS-formatted drive already maintains. Almost all primary as well as secondary storage drives on Windows are formatted in NTFS, which means they have a Master File Table (MFT). This is an internal log of every single file on the volume, tracking its name, size, physical location, and timestamp. The MFT is updated as you make changes to the files and folders on your drive.

item.title: I gave up on Samsung's Upcycle program and turned my old Galaxy phone into a Jellyfin media server
item.itunes:title: I gave up on Samsung's Upcycle program and turned my old Galaxy phone into a Jellyfin media server
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Old phones are among the most ignored devices in my household. Their processor or battery becomes too weak for daily tasks, and some apps stop supporting the old Android versions. Or, family members upgrade to a better version. Whatever the reason is, a slightly weak but still functioning device is out of commission. Since I've already experimented with small home server projects, repurposing old phones was my next goal.

I had an old Samsung Galaxy phone lying around, and I wasn’t eager for the Samsung Upcycle program to turn it into e-waste. Rooting the phone has its perks, but I didn't want to risk ruining a working phone. I experimented with a few apps, deployed a Jellyfin container, and even did package installs. Finally, the server was up and running, but it was one of the most frustrating projects I've ever done.

Building a server from an old phone

Multiple approaches

As I mentioned above, there are multiple ways you can approach a project like this. You can root your phone to wipe the Android operating system and then install something like Debian on it. After that, you can install Jellyfin, map the correct ports, and then host the tool. This option gives you the maximum resources because you don't need to run an emulated OS inside Android.

The non-root option requires an application like Termux or Podroid to create an isolated space. Termux provides a Linux-like userspace, while Podroid supplies you with all the tools and has preconfigured Docker and other container management systems. You can even run a lightweight installation of Ubuntu inside Termux with PRoot, and then install tools there. This option is safer, doesn't increase your chances of bricking a working phone, and is more convenient.

I turned my old phone into a device that does something my $300 smart home gadgets can't

Turns out I haven't been utilizing my old phone enough.

1
By  Anurag Singh

However, there is a significant performance drop when using tools like Termux or Podroid for demanding setups like a media server. The latter uses a form of virtualization, and that's great for resource control and a few other things. But it's certainly not suitable for very old or weak smartphones.

Podroid was my first pick

But it turned out to be a menace

I've built a phone server with Podroid that hosts OmniTools and BentoPDF. Both of them are set up as Docker containers, and Podroid includes the Docker system by default. I thought it would be the same easy method, and spinning up a container doesn't take much time. But it was the least of my problems because running Jellyfin as a container invited multiple problems. I had to factor in bind mounts, assign ports, and handle a few other aspects of networking, which felt infuriating.

Initially, the container would deploy without a problem, but would fail health checks and stop automatically. I stopped the health checks by modifying the commands, and then a new problem arose. The tool needed port forwarding, so I had to use ADB to implement that. Jellyfin’s web interface launched after that, and I even tried to do the initial configuration. But it was very slow and unresponsive.

A battered screen didn't stop me from turning my old Samsung phone into a functional home server

It's now an important part of my home lab

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

The next idea was to install the Jellyfin package directly and avoid Docker altogether. Sadly, this route turned out to be more problematic. The API would load and get stuck at migration, making me wait for 30 minutes or more to launch the page. I ditched this setup for Termux, and it made the whole media server project possible.

Termux was pretty straightforward, and I first set up an Ubuntu system using PRoot. Then, I installed all the necessary components, added the necessary repositories, and installed Jellyfin inside this system. There was some additional effort to map the ports and allow the server to access the phone storage contents. Finally, it was ready to serve content over port 8096.

My phone works as a media server

Fit for basic streaming demands

After the web portal launched, I quickly configured the server and did a few tweaks to allow it to access the phone storage. I created a new library and then set it up for both photo and video content. My old phone has a lot of photos, videos, and some old anime, and it's a perfect concoction for local streaming. I can use it to reminisce about old days, view a slideshow of thousands of images, or play anime or other downloaded media on it.

I tested the video files present on it, and 1080p streaming didn't crash the server. Videos played smoothly, and even 1.5x and 2x playback didn't overload the server. But accessing local storage is only one aspect of a media server. I can use SMB to fetch video files from another network storage. I could also use a USB hard drive, but the phone has only one USB port, which becomes a challenge for any other task.

I used Plex and Jellyfin for a month, and there's one clear winner for true hardware ownership

Your media server shouldn't need the cloud.

10
By  Jasmine Mannan

You might need ADB for troubleshooting, and you will have to use the phone in plugged-in mode. So, the single USB port becomes a challenge that only network accessible storage can solve. However, the hardware has its limits, and the setup cannot handle demanding transcoding workloads. Jellyfin has to rely on the limited CPU cores for everything, and it's suitable for basic direct playback. Rooted devices can perform slightly better, but they carry a huge risk.

Repurposing your phone

I never paid attention to the media server aspect of a smartphone. It was difficult to get the project working on a non-rooted phone, but I eventually found success. The overall performance isn’t close to a mini-PC and more like a medium-grade SBC, at least on my phone. I’m happy that the server doesn’t crash like it did when I tried running Jellyfin on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. However, your phone has to be in plugged-in mode if you want 24/7 availability, and unless it's very old, it probably has overcharge protection built in. Connecting physical storage is also not possible, but you can use a large-capacity SD card if your phone has a slot.

Termux

Termux is a terminal emulator app for Android OS.

Check Termux on Github

item.title: I hibernated my PC every day for five years, and my SSD paid the price
item.itunes:title: I hibernated my PC every day for five years, and my SSD paid the price
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Microsoft disables hibernation by default in Windows 11, and my five-year testing finally revealed why that might be a good thing. My 250GB boot drive, a Samsung 970 EVO Plus, sits at exactly 90 percent health today despite hibernation after work every weekday. To the average home user, that's perfectly acceptable wear on a five-year-old drive, but for demanding power users, dropping below 90% could prove detrimental to system stability. Despite the robust wear-leveling algorithms and handsome warranties every modern SSD carries, there's more than one reason hibernating a Windows 11 machine is best avoided in favor of regular shutdowns.

Your SSD will outlive your PC — unless you ignore these Windows habits

From massive downloads to nearly full drives, everything has an impact on your SSD's lifespan

1
By  Kazim Alvi

The test results aren't cause for concern by themselves

Hibernation has a negligible impact on drive health, but it's noticeable nonetheless

By design, hibernation writes the system status currently stored in the RAM to a temporary file called hiberfil.sys on your boot drive. So, each hibernation write shouldn't exceed the total installed RAM capacity on your machine, which is 32GB in my case. Drive wear metrics from CrystalDiskInfo revealed my boot drive has been powered on for 16,040 hours, while the storage controller endured 53,341 gigabytes of total host writes. Sure, all that isn't from hibernation alone, but it equates to around 4.6 years of daily hibernation with 32GB written each time.

That massive daily memory dump consumes 7.79 percent of the drive's endurance limit each year from sleep states alone. Samsung guarantees my specific NVMe drive for 150 terabytes written over a five-year limited warranty period, which was class-leading for its time and a big reason why the drive health still registers at 90%. Regular usage eats into this limit too, meaning you might hit the endurance wall and physically kill the drive long before the warranty expires. item.title: I used a free tool to control an Android phone with a malfunctioning screen, and it's a lifesaver for recovery
item.itunes:title: I used a free tool to control an Android phone with a malfunctioning screen, and it's a lifesaver for recovery
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Smartphones have a fairly long lifespan. I have a Redmi phone that's six years old at this point, a Samsung phone that just turned seven, and another that's about three years old. While most of the hardware functions, the first parts to falter usually involve the screen or the USB charging port. The latter is a cheap replacement compared to the screen. A touchscreen phone without a working screen is basically uncontrollable. But I found a workaround with a tool and slowly recovered all the data, emptied the phone, and prepped it for a small home server project.

Phone screens are fragile

You should be prepared beforehand

It's not the first time that I've had a problem with my phone's display. I have had such encounters before where the screen became unresponsive and then blank. There were also accidents when the phone slipped from my hands or pocket and fell on the floor, leaving it with several cracks. But this time, my mum was trying to play a song on YouTube like she always does. The screen appeared purple with visible grid lines and would occasionally go back to white.

She couldn't type anything or press the buttons in the app, and asked me to check it. I immediately recognized the state, knowing very well that it wouldn't work. The first thought was to copy the storage contents to the PC. But the screen was so unresponsive that I couldn't even click the notification to enable file transfer. Clearly, the touchscreen route wouldn't work, and I found a tool to mirror the screen to the PC.

A battered screen didn't stop me from turning my old Samsung phone into a functional home server

It's now an important part of my home lab

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

It needed ADB for it to work, and I hadn't enabled USB debugging on the phone because nobody does. If you're ignorant like me, you'll have to deal with the same ordeal. It's a setting that can open doors to file transfer, troubleshooting, and much more. I connected a mouse to the phone via an OTG adapter and somehow managed to enable developer options and USB debugging. I also enabled MTP after connecting the phone to my PC with a USB cable.

Copying personal files

Mirroring the phone screen to my PC

The first thing that I did was to copy all the files from personal folders to my PC. It was fairly easy and the first thing to do because the phone had a lot of photos and screenshots. Thereafter, I could go the traditional ADB route to connect to the phone and then use commands to modify settings. But that is tedious and requires me to learn a lot of commands. I found a GitHub tool called scrcpy that could mirror the phone screen via ADB.

It bundles the ADB packages by default, and I didn't have to deal with any of it. Simply extract the archive and then open a terminal window. Navigate to the tool’s directory and run it with the scrcpy command. It'll automatically start a session, and the phone screen will light up. It caused a new problem because my screen was experiencing ghost touches and was not responding correctly. So, I tweaked the command a bit to make the tool work in locked mode.

scrcpy -S -w -d

After that, I could access the interface and move on to the rest. For starters, you could remove the apps you don't need, sign out, and remove personal accounts. Additional cleanup jobs include removing personal files or apps. All these things let you tidy the phone if you want to send it for a repair and worry about personal data loss.

I replaced my Raspberry Pi with an old phone, and it handled everything I threw at it

Raspberry Pi is no longer the best hardware for tinkerers.

6
By  Anurag Singh

The tools run the session via the terminal, but you get a GUI interface to work with. Surprisingly, the screen is flipped to the other side, and some controls and toggles feel weird. But it's not a huge problem, and you can easily navigate the interface with a mouse and keyboard. I used it to enable wireless USB debugging and pair the phone with it. You can even use the phone interface to create a backup file and then restore it after you get the screen fixed. However, I had another thing on my mind.

Building a home server with an Android phone

Removing bloatware to free up space for tools

Samsung phones have a lot of bloatware, and it's not easy to remove it via the phone UI route. Scrcpy was very helpful with screen mirroring and makes it incredibly simple for a lot of phone-related actions. For more control, ADB is essential to remove packages. Rather than using ADB commands, I used the Universal Android Debloater (UAD) tool. It categorizes the packages into safe, unsafe, and a few other buckets, and the GUI interface makes it easy to both purge and restore packages when needed.

I turned my old phone into a device that does something my $300 smart home gadgets can't

Turns out I haven't been utilizing my old phone enough.

1
By  Anurag Singh

I was able to free up about 14GB of internal storage space with this approach to personal files, apps, and packages. Then I installed Podroid, which uses virtualization to set up a Docker system. I deployed BentoPDF and OmniTools and tested a few other tools, but these two remained permanent. You can build a similar server after a deep package cleanup on your phone to make space for Podroid setup.

Easy recovery

USB debugging is turned off for security purposes, but it's the most helpful thing when your phone screen malfunctions. Enabling it is the key to opening the door for future phone control. If you notice any kind of screen flickering, spots, or the dreaded green lines, enable USB debugging immediately. Then, you can use scrcpy to mirror the phone screen interface, plan recovery, and enable other settings like MTP for file transfer. Controlling a faulty display becomes painless with scrcpy and a single launch command. You can use it in wireless mode, but it needs initial setup, and the input delay is somewhat frustrating.

item.itunes:title: We thought Chinese companies could save us from the DRAM crisis, but they're charging just as much as the big three
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For most of the past year or two, PC builders that have been priced out of DDR5 have had one name to squarely pin their hopes and dreams of cheap memory to. CXMT, China's largest DRAM manufacturer, was supposed to be the fourth supplier that broke up the big three: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The thought was, once CXMT ramps up their own manufacturing to fill the void that those companies left in hopes of securing the AI bag, cheaper memory would become available for consumers. It's a nice thought, but the truth is, CXMT is pricing like the companies it was supposed to undercut, and if you were holding off on a build in hopes that Chinese memory would rescue your budget, you'll be waiting for a long time.

The RAM stick is dying, and the replacement is something most PC builders have never seen

There may be a new memory standard coming to town soon

28
By  Abhinav Raj

The CXMT discount was never going to be massive

The savings were thin to begin with

Credit: Hardware Unboxed (YouTube)

Performance isn't an issue with CXMT-made RAM, and that's been proven in real-world tests. Hardware Unboxed purchased a KingBank 32GB DDR5-6000 CL36 kit in Australia earlier this year, where kits with CXMT chips were among the cheapest DDR5 on the shelf. In gaming, it kept pace with a premium G.Skill kit built on SK Hynix chips.

The KingBank kit sold for about 599 AUD, against roughly 649 AUD for comparable kits using Samsung, SK Hynix, or Micron chips. That's a saving of under 8%, at a time when the same class of kit had multiplied in price over just a few months. Pricing seemed more aggressive when these kits first went on sale, but they've shifted within weeks of going on sale. If you looked at headlines from even earlier, the prices that were being floated were a fraction of the going rate, but buyers never actually saw those prices at retail.

Unified memory is quietly killing SO-DIMM, and mini PCs prove it's already happening

Speed over freedom

By  João Carrasqueira

CXMT makes the chips, but someone else makes the actual sticks of RAM

There are a few parties involved here

CXMT manufactures DRAM chips, and it sells some finished modules of its own, mostly for servers. The kits most builders would buy, from brands like KingBank and Gloway, come from module makers. item.title: This useful app brought my Plex library directly to my Google TV home screen
item.itunes:title: This useful app brought my Plex library directly to my Google TV home screen
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
While I typically stream content with my Apple TV 4K, I've recently spent some time experimenting with my Hisense U8H TV's built-in Google TV operating system. When it isn't lagging (which happens more often than I'd like), it's actually not that bad, and I've grown to really appreciate the open nature of Android-based Google TV.

With that in mind, I've been hunting for an app that better integrates my Plex library with the TV's default operating system, allowing me to browse my self-hosted movies and TV shows from my TV's main screen the same way I search through apps like Netflix, Disney+, and Prime.

Surprisingly, that's exactly what Google TV launcher Dispatch does. While the experience is far from perfect, there's plenty to like about Dispatch's stripped-back UI and Plex integration.

There's a lot to like about Dispatch's Plex integration and overall simplicity

The ad-free launcher feels kind of empty (but in a good way)

First it's important to note that Dispatch isn't free. While the launcher comes with a 14-day free trial, it costs $1/month or $10 for a lifetime license, which might be difficult for some people to swallow. Dispatch offers a very low-key, ad-free look that I really appreciate. In a way, the simplicity reminds me of Apple's tvOS, only without the never-ending advertisements.

The marquee feature that attracted me is Dispatch's Plex integration, which is great for users looking for a new way to explore their self-hosted movie and TV library. The launcher directly integrates all of your Plex content on its home screen, allowing you to navigate through your content in the same way that you would Netflix or Prime. Obviously, the Watch Next list and Recommendations are based on content you have on your self-hosted Plex server (random TV shows and movies won't show up).

For other content, you can toggle rows on/off on Dispatch's homepage. So, for example, if you don't subscribe to Disney+, you can remove content suggestions for that app so you aren't constantly bombarded with movie and TV show suggestions for a platform you don't even subscribe to.

You can even hide all media if you want, leaving a simple navigation row of installed apps in the top-left corner of the screen. Speaking of the top-left corner, this is where all your Favorite Apps live. When you highlight a specific app, you'll see what Dispatch calls an App Peek, offering "context-appropriate" media that you can press Enter on to open the app and browse that content. It's a clever feature and the type of thing I'd expect from Apple, not a relatively unknown third-party Google TV launcher developer.

There's also the Home Feed, where Plex's content is integrated alongside other traditional streaming apps. The traditional Google TV Control Center has also been revamped with a more Apple-like look, too. You'll find Settings features like the Power Menu, Recent Apps, your network, and more here. It's a bit difficult to navigate at first, but I quickly got the hang of it.

The navigation experience isn't perfect

I've encountered a few instances of lag

At times, Dispatch's layout can feel a bit barren, especially if you're used to Google TV's busier home screen, but I've gotten used to it over the past few days. I've also found it a bit laggy at times, though that might be my aging Hisense U8H, or the fact that I need to clear its cache yet again (I feel like I need to do this every few weeks).

I haven't tried this yet, but Dispatch offers Graphics Modes settings that aim to improve performance on lower-end Android TV devices, including High, Medium, and Low. If I still encounter performance issues, I plan to switch to Low, which tones down the launcher's overall presentation, including animations and image size. There's even a useful Wallpaper Mode that allows you to select any photo as the backdrop for your TV. However, it lacks native Google Photos album integration like the stock Google TV OS.

Credit: Dispatch

In a way, I'm only scratching the surface with this story because Dispatch offers a ridiculous amount of features and customization options. Unfortunately, there still isn't an easy way to set a third-party launcher to open when you turn on your Google TV. To do this, you'll need to use ADB (Android Debug Bridge)to disable the stock Google TV launcher.

This is an issue with every third-party Google TV launcher I've ever used. I get around it by pinning the Dispatch app at the top of the default Google TV launcher, so it boots up as soon as I turn on my TV. If you're tired of the never-ending ads in the stock Google TV launcher, Dispatch offers a surprisingly refreshing change that I've come to really appreciate.

Dispatch requires you to sign in to your Google account. The team behind the launcher says this is necessary to track the 14-day trial without forcing users to pre-purchase the app. I don't see this as a big deal, but I can understand some users having privacy concerns.

Additionally, in order for background syncing to work, you'll need to navigate to Settings > Apps > Special App Access > Energy Optimization > look for Dispatch and turn off Energy Optimization.

Dispatch
See at Google Play Store

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The best aspect of ESP32 boards, aside from their inexpensive price tags, is their versatility. Toss in a couple of resistors, capacitors, and breadboards, and you can train your circuit-building skills with them. Or, you could arm your tiny tinkering board with a sensor or two, write some firmware via ESPHome, and turn it into another smart device for Home Assistant. Heck, even on their own, there’s a lot you can do with an ESP32, especially once you look into other boards besides the base model.

Take the ESP32-S3, as an example. Besides its superior processing capabilities, this tiny gizmo ships with two USB ports, and one of them makes this tiny microcontroller capable of emulating typical USB accessories.

Why I stopped buying official ESP32 developer boards, and what I use instead

They're reference designs for a reason.

5
By  Adam Conway

The native USB OTG port on the ESP32-S3 is the star of the show

Its Bluetooth provisions are just as useful for DIY USB devices

If you look closely at an ESP32-S3, you’ll spot a port marked as UART. That’s the conventional port for serial communication, and it’s what you’d typically use to connect the microcontroller to a PC when you want to flash it with custom firmware. But what we’re concerned with is the other USB port.

Typically labeled as USB, this port connects to the ESP32-S3’s USB On-the-Go controller, which, in turn, lets your PC recognize it as any other I/O accessory. Sure, you can technically still use it to program the board thanks to the JTAG controller connected to the port. But since it can mimic typical USB devices, you can turn your ESP32-S3 into anything from a DIY USB mouse and joystick to a full-fledged keyboard, joystick, and even a storage device, albeit a painfully low-capacity one. Heck, you can even use it to run macros every time a button or a sensor hooked up to the microcontroller gets triggered, and that’s easily my favorite use case for its native USB port.

Good ol’ Arduino IDE is enough to flash the ESP32-S3 with firmware

I went with a simple KY-023 module for the experiment

Since my DIY ESP32-S3 macro setup is something I wanted to pair with my PC and not Home Assistant, I decided to ditch ESPHome and go with Arduino IDE instead. I also wanted to try out an analog stick module (specifically, the KY-023) from a cheap sensor kit, so I used the following connection table to hook it up to the ESP32-S3 via some jumper wires:

Then, I used the UART USB port on the microcontroller to connect it to my PC and tweaked the port setting within the Arduino IDE to ensure that it detects the ESP32-S3. As for the code, I figured I could start off with a simple automation that launches the File Explorer on my Windows 11 PC every time I press down on the analog stick. So, the overall code looks something like this:

#include <Arduino.h>
#include "USB.h"
#include "USBHIDKeyboard.h"
USBHIDKeyboard Keyboard;
constexpr uint8_t JOY_SW_PIN = 6;
constexpr uint32_t debounceTimeMs = 60;
bool previousButtonState = HIGH;
uint32_t lastPressTime = 0;
void openFileExplorer() {
  Keyboard.press(KEY_LEFT_GUI);
  Keyboard.press('e');
  delay(50);
  Keyboard.release('e');
  Keyboard.release(KEY_LEFT_GUI);
}
void setup() {
  pinMode(JOY_SW_PIN, INPUT_PULLUP);
  Keyboard.begin();
  USB.begin();
  delay(1500);
}
void loop() {
  bool currentButtonState = digitalRead(JOY_SW_PIN);
  if (previousButtonState == HIGH &&
      currentButtonState == LOW &&
      millis() - lastPressTime >= debounceTimeMs) {
    lastPressTime = millis();
    openFileExplorer();
  }
  previousButtonState = currentButtonState;
  delay(5);
}

Specifically, the #include "USBHIDKeyboard.h" snippet brings in the library responsible for letting the native USB mimic a keyboard, while the openFileExplorer() function is responsible for ensuring that the File Explorer shortcut (Win+E) gets triggered when a new button press is detected. Finally, the millis() - lastPressTime >= debounceTimeMs line ensures that my microcontroller doesn’t continuously send the macro signal if I leave the analog stick pressed.

Once I’d uploaded the firmware to my tiny tinkering companion, I unplugged the cable from the UART port. Then, I plugged it into the native USB port, and sure enough, my DIY macro setup worked without a hitch.

The macros become more useful once you toss more button modules into the mix

On its own, this experiment can't really improve my productivity, but the real fun begins once I start building extra actions on top of my current macros. For example, rather than launching the File Explorer, I could map the Ctrl+Z option to the key press. In fact, the KY-023 is technically an analog stick, so I could also map different actions for the X and Y axis movements.

And that’s just one module. With a breadboard, I could easily pair multiple buttons with the ESP32-S3. Heck, I could even hook a slightly expensive touchscreen display to the ESP32-S3, program the latter to show different icons on the screen, and use their coordinates to trigger different actions every time I tap the display.

item.title: Nvidia's DGX Spark is getting a 64GB RAM variant to make running local models more affordable
item.itunes:title: Nvidia's DGX Spark is getting a 64GB RAM variant to make running local models more affordable
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Nvidia launches 64GB DGX Spark using the same GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip as the 128GB model.
  • 64GB Spark is priced at $4,999 as a budget entry option vs. the pricier 128GB model.
  • Sync Cluster Assistant lets you link Sparks to share RAM (e.g., 2×64GB→128GB or 4×128GB→512GB).

If you're an avid AI user or developer, you're probably already running LLMs on local hardware. You may also be familiar with the Nvidia DGX Spark, the AI and graphics giant's answer for people who want to skip the cloud and run AI at home and in the office. Now, the company is pulling back the curtain on a new, cheaper 64GB Spark variant, and it's coming soon.

The Nvidia DGX Spark gets a small but mighty 64GB version

You can also sync up multiple Sparks into one cohesive unit

As announced on the Nvidia website, the DGX Spark is getting a 64GB RAM version. This one is designed to be a budget, entry-level version of the Spark versus the 128GB model you can currently purchase. Fortunately, it uses the exact same GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip as the higher-end 128GB model, meaning that the 64GB version has the same processing speed and architectural features as its bigger brother.

The 128GB model used to sell for around $4,000 MSRP, but the recent price fluctuations mean you see it more around the $7,000 mark these days. As such, Nvidia has released this 64GB version for $4,999 to make its hardware more accessible for smaller budgets.

Nvidia also took the time to show off the Sync Cluster Assistant. This allows people to hook up several DGX Sparks to combine their RAM for even more powerful computing. The obvious benefit here is that you can stick two 64GB Sparks together to make a unified system with 128GB of shared memory, but the example chart that Nvidia created showed tying four of the 128GB models together for a mighty 512GB system.

The Nvidia DGX Spark will arrive from Acer, Asus, Dell, Gigabyte, HP, and MSI starting October 23rd.

Apple's M3 Ultra Mac Studio manages things no other PC is capable of

It's expensive, but you won't find this kind of power elsewhere.

5
By  Adam Conway
